query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the tungsten content in high-entropy alloy protective coatings enhances wear performance by promoting the dynamic formation of an ultra-fine, nanocrystalline surface layer during sliding, which serves as a barrier to both abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., FeCoCrNiAlWₓ) with low tungsten content (x near 0) and a standard microstructure without a pronounced ultrafine surface layer.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the tungsten content in the alloy composition from x ≈ 0 to x ≈ 0.8 during coating fabrication.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted at room temperature under controlled load conditions with consistent surface preparations to ensure uniformity in the coating microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dynamically stabilized ultra-fine nanocrystalline (or amorphous) surface layer at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: Higher tungsten levels enhance localized frictional heating and thermal stability at the sliding interface. This promotes a microstructural refinement via dynamic amorphization, which reduces the generation of abrasive particles and diminishes adhesive wear by acting as an effective barrier.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with elevated tungsten content will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate relative to the low-tungsten baseline. Microscopic analysis should reveal a more pronounced ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer on the worn surfaces of the high-W coatings.
generation.baseline: A coating with low tungsten content (x near 0) that does not efficiently form the protective ultrafine surface layer, resulting in higher friction and greater wear rates.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for tungsten contents in the range of 0 to 0.8 under dry sliding conditions at room temperature. The influence of the effect under high-temperature or lubricated conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of tungsten content at which the wear-resisting benefits saturate, as well as the universality of the mechanism across different HEA systems, requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of FeCoCrNiAlWₓ coatings with tungsten contents incremented from 0 to 0.8. Conduct standardized dry sliding wear tests under identical load and temperature conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze the near-surface layer of the worn coatings.
measurements: Friction coefficients during the running-in and steady state phases
Wear rates (mm³/N-m) for each tungsten level
Microstructural characterization (grain size, phase identification) of the worn surface layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if increasing tungsten content does not produce a statistically significant reduction in the friction coefficient and wear rate and if no corresponding ultra-fine nanocrystalline surface layer is detected in the high-tungsten coatings relative to the baseline.

Figure 8 illustrates the FeCoCrNiAlWx high-entropy alloy cladding coating with friction coefficient curves, as the W content increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8. The friction coefficients of the cladding coatings with different W compositions display significant fluctuations during the running-in stage of the friction experiment, gradually stabilizing over time. During the stable phase, as the W content rises from x = 0 to x = 0.8, the average friction coefficients of the cladding coatings are 0.669, 0.664, 0.617, 0.544, and 0.527, respectively. Overall, the friction coefficient decreases with increasing W content, indicating that the incorporation of W improves the wear resistance of the cladding coating. It is noteworthy that the friction coefficients for x = 0 are similar with x = 0.2, suggesting minimal enhancement of wear resistance with low W content. However, the friction coefficients for x = 0.6 are close with x = 0.8; this suggests that a further increase in W content results in a saturation effect on enhancing wear resistance.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
